battle.title: Queue Up!
battle.description: Producers, consumers, duplicates and dead letters.

questions.text: What is the main benefit of putting a message queue between a producer and a consumer?
options: The consumer is guaranteed to reply in real time
They are decoupled: the producer does not wait, and the queue buffers bursts
Messages can never be processed more than once
The producer learns the processing result immediately
questions.answer: They are decoupled: the producer does not wait, and the queue buffers bursts
questions.explanation: A queue lets the producer hand off work and move on while consumers process at their own pace. It adds asynchrony, so you do not get an immediate result or a real-time guarantee.

questions.text: Checkout must not wait for a slow email provider after an order is placed. What should you do?
options: Publish an order-placed message and let a worker send the email
Call the email API inside the checkout request
Raise the HTTP timeout on checkout
Make the browser poll the database until the email is sent
questions.answer: Publish an order-placed message and let a worker send the email
questions.explanation: Queuing the work makes checkout fast and lets the worker retry if the provider is down. A synchronous call ties checkout latency and availability to the email service.

questions.text: A queue offers at-least-once delivery. What must the consumer be prepared for?
options: Never receiving a message at all
Always receiving messages in strict global order
Receiving the same message more than once
questions.answer: Receiving the same message more than once
questions.explanation: At-least-once means no loss but possible redelivery (for example after a missed ack), so processing should be idempotent. Exactly-once is much harder and usually achieved by deduplicating on the consumer side.

questions.text: What is a dead-letter queue used for?
options: Storing messages for consumers that are currently offline
Holding messages that repeatedly failed, so they stop blocking the main queue
Giving high-priority messages a faster lane
questions.answer: Holding messages that repeatedly failed, so they stop blocking the main queue
questions.explanation: After a set number of failed attempts, a poison message is moved aside for inspection instead of being retried forever. Buffering for offline consumers is what the normal queue already does.

questions.text: A payment queue delivers some messages twice. What does this program print for the naive total and the total with deduplication by id?
questions.explanation: The naive sum counts duplicates: 10 + 20 + 20 + 5 + 10 = 65. Skipping ids already seen counts each payment once: 10 + 20 + 5 = 35. Idempotent consumers make at-least-once delivery safe.
